open-question.question: The mission re-evaluates every one of the 35 invariants in today's `CLAUDE.md` and compresses each to its rule, its reason, and the retired forms that must not return. May a re-evaluation end in a rule itself being dropped or changed, for example one found obsolete or one that only records an accepted limitation, or does the mission change only wording and placement, every rule standing exactly as it binds today?
open-question.alternative: No rule is dropped or changed: every one of the 35 invariants keeps binding exactly as it does today. Re-evaluation cuts only text that binds nothing (mechanics already stated in the runtime files, field measurements, dates, the history of how a form came about) and moves each rule to its home. An entry that records an accepted limitation ("accepted as it stands", "accepted as never to be changed") stays as a rule, compressed to what must not be changed and why. Candidates for retirement are not recorded anywhere. The mission's diff can be reviewed as a pure move and compression: no tool, test, runtime file, or behaviour changes, and a reviewer has only to check that every rule survives, so the risk of losing a design decision while rewriting 145,667 bytes is the lowest of any option. Rules whose subject no longer stands in the tree (the pre-split missions, the pre-flip TASKS_DONE.md note) and entries kept only to stop a limitation being "fixed" are carried into the new tree as they are, so part of the bulk the byte budgets must hold is text the re-evaluation already judged dead, and the goal's "every invariant is re-evaluated" yields nothing beyond compression.

alternative.id: Wording only, candidates kept for later

open-question.alternative: This mission changes only wording and placement, every rule binding as it does today, as in the wording-only option. Where re-evaluation finds a rule obsolete or one that only records an accepted limitation, the runner leaves the rule standing in its new home and records it as a retirement candidate, with the reason, in one draft under ideas/ for a later mission to decide. Keeps this mission's diff a pure move and compression while not wasting the judgment the re-evaluation forms: the candidates reach a later mission as a ready list, where each drop can be decided on its own with the tree already in place. The dead text still has to fit inside this mission's byte budgets, and the draft is one more document the tree must point at and the update skill must keep honest until a later mission takes it up, which nothing schedules.

alternative.id: Drop obsolete rules, decided up front

open-question.alternative: A rule may be dropped, never changed, and only when its subject no longer exists in the tree or the history it guards is closed (for example the pre-split missions and the pre-flip TASKS_DONE.md note); every other rule, accepted-limitation entries included, keeps binding exactly as today. Each drop is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, the review pass authoring one open question per candidate, so the recorded decisions list every rule that leaves. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Removes the clearest dead weight from the tree while every drop is a recorded, revertible decision rather than a runner's call, and the rule that stops a limitation being "fixed" is left untouched, so no behaviour can drift. Adds a round of questions before derivation for a handful of small drops, and an obsolete-looking rule may still bind something (the TASKS_DONE.md note also says no runner is to read or recreate the file), so each candidate needs care that a compressed retired-forms line could have given at no cost.

alternative.id: Drop obsolete and limitation rules, decided up front

open-question.alternative: A rule may be dropped, never changed, when it is obsolete or when it only records an accepted limitation (the commit tool's exit-128 retry accepted as it stands, the hand-rendered attribute rule, markup accepted in an alternative's text, the unbounded show print); a dropped limitation entry leaves behaviour as it is and stops forbidding a later fix. Each drop is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per candidate. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Cuts the largest class of text that binds no current behaviour, the accepted-limitation records written in the latest mission's tasks, so the tree states what the code must do rather than every fix that was weighed and declined. An accepted-limitation entry exists precisely so a later editor does not "fix" what was left on purpose; dropping it removes that guard, and a later mission may re-measure and re-decide something already settled, at a cost the drop saved only in bytes.

A rule may be dropped, never changed, when its subject no longer exists in the tree, under one criterion recorded as a decision of this mission; the task runner compressing that area applies it and names each dropped rule, with its reason, in its task's verified bar. Accepted-limitation entries and every other rule keep binding as today. No runtime file, tool, or test changes. Removes dead rules without a question round before derivation, since applying one narrow, checkable criterion (the subject is gone from the tree) is a runner's job, and every drop still shows in a commit body and its diff. A design decision leaves the project's record by a runner's judgment rather than a recorded answer, and a runner reading "subject gone" loosely can drop a rule that still binds (a retired form that must not return is exactly a rule whose subject is gone); how much is left to runners also depends on the axis the Placement decision timing question owns.

alternative.id: Drop or change rules, docs only

open-question.alternative: Re-evaluation may drop a rule (obsolete or limitation-only) or change what it binds, narrowing, loosening, or merging rules where it finds one wrong or redundant, but only where the change needs no edit to a runtime file, tool, test, or build: the rules change what a later editor may do, never what the code does now. Each drop or change is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per rule. Gives the re-evaluation its full value at the level of the rules themselves, so overlapping or contradictory invariants written over many missions can be reconciled into a smaller, coherent set rather than faithfully compressed, while the plugin's behaviour stays exactly as shipped. Many questions may be raised across 35 rules before derivation, lengthening the mission's preparation, and a rule changed without touching the code it governs can leave code that the new rule no longer explains or that now contradicts it until a later mission aligns them.

alternative.id: Drop or change rules with the code

open-question.alternative: Re-evaluation may drop or change any rule, and a changed rule carries the change to the runtime files, tools, tests, and rebuilt host trees it governs in this mission, so rule and code stay in step. Each drop or change is decided in this mission before tasks are derived, one open question per rule. Every rule in the new tree states exactly what the code does, with no rule left wrong or out of step, and a defect the re-evaluation exposes is fixed where it is found rather than deferred. Turns a documentation mission into a plugin-behaviour mission of unbounded size across all of core/ and the host trees, overlapping the defined mission_project-defined-knowledge-placement/ that changes the context-reading runners and finish, and mixes behaviour changes into a diff that is otherwise reviewable as moves and compression.

open-question.question: The four `README.md` nodes under `core/tools/`, `core/shared/`, `core/skills/`, and `core/agents/` are kept out of the host trees by each host's `exclude` list, with no change to the build's Python. The build's `host-name-in-core` and `old-word-in-core` checks, however, scan every file under `core/` whether or not a host excludes it, so a node there fails the build when it names a host or holds the word "milestone", and several of today's invariants do both in their rule or their retired forms. Do those four nodes obey the two checks as they stand, with any rule text that must name a host or a milestone reworded or stated in a node outside `core/`, or do the checks change to skip the nodes, setting aside the no-build-change clause?
open-question.alternative: The two checks stay exactly as they are and scan the four nodes like every other file under `core/`. The no-build-change clause holds. Every rule placed in a `core/` node is worded so that it names no host and carries no "milestone". A host is named by its mechanism (its tool names, config keys, file names, or "a host that dispatches in capped rounds") or by its definition directory path (`scripts/hosts/<host>/`, which the check reads as an identifier and passes). A milestone citation becomes a date, a commit hash, or a mission path, or it is dropped as history. No rule text leaves `core/` because it names a host or a milestone. Nothing in the build, its docstring, or its tests changes, and the rule that `core/` names no host stays in force with no exception. Every core rule also stays whole in the node of the folder it chiefly governs, as the recorded spanning-rule decision requires. Today only five invariants name a host and eight carry the word "milestone" (eleven occurrences), so the rewording has a known, bounded size. Some rules read worse or lose precision. The per-host halves of the slot rule (the capped-round Codex value, the Claude Code refused-dispatch step, the Antigravity bare agent names) and the "AGENTS.md in the Antigravity and Codex trees" clause have to be written around the hosts they describe. Milestone citations such as "milestone 44" or "milestone_01–27" point at history no missions-tool query lists, so a date or hash in their place is harder to follow, and dropping them loses evidence. How much of that evidence may be dropped also depends on the scope the rule-retirement question settles.

The two checks stay exactly as they are and scan the four nodes. The no-build-change clause holds. Text that can be reworded without losing meaning is reworded as in the in-place option, milestone citations included. Rule text that has to name a host is stated in a node outside `core/`, and the `core/` node points at it. The chief candidate is the per-host values of the slot rule and the host-tree differences, stated in a `scripts/hosts/README.md` node (a name the build reads nowhere, since it reads no file standing directly in `scripts/hosts/`) or in the root `CLAUDE.md`. The build stays unchanged and the host-neutral rule for `core/` stays exceptionless. The rules that must name a host end up beside the host definitions, slot values, and dated hands-on blocks they describe, where someone editing a host looks first, so they are worded naturally instead of written around the hosts. One rule's text can end up split across two nodes: a host-neutral half in a `core/` node and a host-specific half under `scripts/hosts/`. That pulls against the recorded rule that a spanning rule is stated once and whole in its chief folder's node, with pointers elsewhere, and it requires a judgment, rule by rule, about which half is the rule. It also adds a node, or root text inside the 20,000-byte root budget, that the covered-folder rule did not require.

The no-build-change clause is set aside for this one point. Both `host-name-in-core` and `old-word-in-core` skip any `core/` file that every host definition's `exclude` list names, so they scan exactly the files that reach at least one host tree. The four nodes are listed in every host's `exclude` and are then written freely: host names and milestone citations stay as the compressed rules need them. The build's docstring and its rendering test are updated to state and pin the skip. It is the principled rule. The checks exist to keep rendered trees host-neutral and free of the retired word, and a file no host renders cannot leak into one. Making that explicit costs one shared predicate (`is_excluded` already exists) and names no particular file, so a later non-rendered file under `core/` needs no further build change. The checks' guarantee becomes only as good as the `exclude` lists. A runtime file excluded from every host by mistake escapes both scans silently, and the rule against naming a host gains a carve-out that the "runtime files name no host" invariant has to state. It also breaks the recorded decision that the nodes need no change to the build's Python, and the `slot-declaration` check, which also scans all of `core/`, would still count a `{{SLOT}}` written in a node as a slot's use unless it is given the same skip.

The no-build-change clause is set aside for this one point. Both `host-name-in-core` and `old-word-in-core` skip exactly the files named `README.md` directly inside `core/tools/`, `core/shared/`, `core/skills/`, and `core/agents/`, a fixed path set written into the build, which can also fail when one of those nodes is missing from any host's `exclude` list. Every other `core/` file, any other excluded one included, is scanned as today. Host names and milestone citations stay in the nodes as the rules need them, and the docstring and rendering test record the exemption. The exemption is as narrow as it can be: only the four nodes the recorded decision created escape the scans, no other file can, and pairing the skip with a check that each node is excluded closes the one way a node could reach a host tree. The compressed rules keep their natural wording, host and milestone evidence included. It hard-codes a documentation layout into the build: adding, renaming, or moving a node under `core/` means editing the build's Python again. It also sets aside the recorded no-build-change clause, and `slot-declaration` would still count a placeholder written in a node unless it is given the same skip.

The no-build-change clause is set aside only for `old-word-in-core`. That check skips the four named `core/` node files, so milestone citations stay as written in them. `host-name-in-core` keeps scanning the nodes unchanged, and every rule text that would name a host is reworded into mechanism terms or stated in a node outside `core/` (`scripts/hosts/README.md` or the root) with a pointer from the `core/` node. It keeps the stronger guarantee, that no file under `core/` names a host, exceptionless, while exempting only the word ban, whose purpose is keeping the retired unit name out of runtime prose. A maintainer node citing history is not runtime prose. The milestone evidence, which no query can recover, stays readable as recorded. It still changes the build's Python against the recorded clause and still carries the host-naming rewording or relocation cost of the two check-obeying options. Two checks that today treat `core/` the same way would then cover different file sets, an asymmetry the build's docstring has to explain.

The no-build-change clause is set aside only for `host-name-in-core`. That check skips the four named `core/` node files, so the slot rule and the host-tree clauses keep naming Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex as written. `old-word-in-core` keeps scanning the nodes unchanged, and every milestone citation in them becomes a date, commit hash, or mission path, or is dropped as history. It exempts exactly the text that is hardest to reword: the per-host halves of the slot rule describe each host's own mechanism and read naturally only by naming the host. The milestone citations, which a date or hash can replace, are reworded, so the retired word stays out of `core/` entirely. It weakens the plugin's central host-neutrality guarantee for `core/`, with a carve-out the "runtime files name no host" invariant must state, to save rewording in five invariants. It changes the build against the recorded clause, and it leaves the two checks covering different file sets. How much milestone evidence may be dropped also depends on the scope the rule-retirement question settles.

open-question.question: Every node holds only the fixed, ordered parts (purpose, rules, commands, pointers), and the mission's pytest check verifies a node's headings against that set. The root `CLAUDE.md` is a node as well, yet it must also hold the bootstrap's `## Mission Workflow` section, the rules on where knowledge lives and how nodes are read, the entries for the root files that cannot carry a header, and the descriptions of `core/`, `hosts/`, `gurita-vscode/`, and `.github/`, each a description with the same parts of its own. Which headings, in which order, does the check allow in the root `CLAUDE.md`, or is the root left out of the heading check?
open-question.alternative: The root is checked against the same four node parts plus one heading of its own: exactly `## Purpose`, `## Rules`, `## Commands`, `## Pointers`, and `## Mission Workflow`, in that order, Purpose and Mission Workflow required and the others present only when filled, Mission Workflow last, where the bootstrap appends it to a file that lacks it. The rules on where knowledge lives and how nodes are read stand as rules inside `## Rules`, and the entries for `VERSION`, `.python-version`, and `AGENTS.md` are said inside the purpose or a rule, as the node structure says of any file. The descriptions of `core/`, `hosts/`, `gurita-vscode/`, and `.github/` stand inside `## Pointers`, one `### <folder>/` heading each beside the pointer lines for the folders with nodes of their own, and each description's own `####` headings are checked against the same four parts and order. The root differs from every other node by exactly one heading, the bootstrap's, which the bootstrap and the extension's offer already key on, so one allowed set and one ordering rule serve the whole tree, and each description sits where that folder's pointer would stand and is checked exactly as a node is. The knowledge-placement directions have no heading of their own and are mixed among the project-wide rules, so a runner looking for which node to read or write must find them inside `## Rules`, and the descriptions push the root to four heading levels and make `## Pointers` most of the file; how many descriptions it holds depends on how the docs folder coverage question settles.

The root is checked against a larger fixed set of its own, in this order: `## Purpose`, `## Rules`, `## Knowledge placement` (where knowledge lives and how nodes are read), `## Root files` (the entries for the files that cannot carry a header), `## Commands`, `## Pointers` (pointer lines only), `## Folder descriptions` holding one `### <folder>/` heading per described folder whose `####` headings are checked against the four node parts and order, and `## Mission Workflow` last. Purpose, Knowledge placement, and Mission Workflow are required, the others present only when filled. Every kind of content only the root holds has a fixed heading a reader, the update skill, or a later plugin following the placement directions can find by name, and the check pins the whole root shape explicitly rather than leaving the extras to be found inside the general parts. The root's set becomes a second, longer list beside the node set that the check, the update skill, and the root's own rules must each keep in step, it departs most from the rule that a node holds only the fixed parts, and its extra headings and depth spend part of the 20,000-byte budget.

The root holds `## Purpose`, `## Rules` (the knowledge-placement and reading rules and the root-file entries inside it), `## Commands`, and `## Pointers` (pointer lines only), then one `## <folder>/` heading per folder the root describes, in path order, each holding `###` headings checked against the four node parts and order as an embedded node, and `## Mission Workflow` last. The check derives the allowed folder headings from the covered folder rule, the tracked top-level folders whose `README.md` name is taken or rendered, so a description of any other folder or a missing one fails. Each description reads as a node one level down, at the same heading depth a node's parts have, so the check verifies a description by the same code it verifies a node with, and the root's heading depth stays at three. The root's top-level set is no longer a fixed list but depends on which folders count as taken or rendered, so the check must compute it from the tree and its list changes whenever a folder's coverage does, for instance by how the docs folder coverage question settles; the knowledge-placement directions again have no heading of their own.

The root is held only partly to the node shape: the check requires `## Purpose` and `## Mission Workflow` and verifies that whichever of `## Rules`, `## Commands`, and `## Pointers` stand appear in that order after Purpose, while every other `##` heading, the knowledge-placement rules, the root-file entries, and the folder descriptions included, is allowed under any name and at any position, and the descriptions' own parts are not checked. No root-specific list has to be agreed or maintained, and a heading the bootstrap appends or a section `finish-mission` adds when it updates "the relevant section" of the context file never fails the check on its name or position. The root can grow new sections the node rule forbids, the way today's file grew from 22,329 bytes after its 2026-09-23 compression back to 171,838 bytes, with only the byte budget to stop it, and the four descriptions standing in for nodes of `core/`, `hosts/`, `gurita-vscode/`, and `.github/` are never verified to hold the parts the node structure decision requires.

The root `CLAUDE.md` is left out of the heading check altogether: it is written to the node structure by convention only, while the mission's other checks (every pointer resolves, every covered folder has a node or a root description, the 20,000-byte budget) still apply to it, and neither its own headings nor its folder descriptions' parts are verified. The simplest check: the heading rule stays one set applied to `README.md` nodes only, and the file whose contents are unlike any other node's, the bootstrap's section included, needs no special case. The node structure decision makes the root a node and gives its folder descriptions the same parts, yet nothing would hold either to them, and the root is the file `finish-mission` edits for lasting changes and the one that has already regrown once after a compression, so the file most exposed to unstructured growth gets no structural guard.

open-question.question: `docs/` serves the plugin's users alone, each of its pages rewritten to user content, while every tracked top-level folder whose `README.md` name is free must be covered by a `README.md` node of its own, a maintainer-facing file of purpose, rules, commands, and pointers that GitHub also shows to anyone browsing the folder. Is `docs/` covered by a `docs/README.md` node standing among the user pages, or by a description in the root `CLAUDE.md`, as the folders whose `README.md` name is taken or rendered are?
open-question.alternative: `docs/` is covered as any folder whose `README.md` name is free: a `docs/README.md` node of the ordinary fixed parts (purpose, rules, commands, pointers), written for maintainers, stands beside the four user pages. It holds the folder's rules (pages carry user content only, mechanics stated by a runtime file, `--help`, docstring, or test are cut and not restated) and its pointers to the pages and to the sources they defer to; the root carries one pointer to it. The covered folder rule and the check apply to `docs/` unchanged, with no exception listed for it. The covered folder rule is applied as recorded with no special case: the check needs no extra entry for `docs/`, the docs rules sit in the folder they govern where someone editing a page finds them, and the root spends only one pointer of its 20,000-byte budget on `docs/`. GitHub renders `docs/README.md` below the file list for anyone browsing the folder, so the users the pages serve alone are shown maintainer rules about cutting mechanics first, which works against the recorded decision that `docs/` serves users alone; it also stands among pages the root `README.md` links users to directly.

`docs/` is treated as a folder whose `README.md` name is reserved, as `.github/` is, and is described by the root `CLAUDE.md` with the same parts as `core/`, `hosts/`, and `gurita-vscode/` are: its purpose, its rules, and pointers to the four pages. No `docs/README.md` is written; the check counts `docs/` among the root-described folders and fails when a tracked `docs/README.md` exists, its message naming the folder's user-only role as the reason. Browsing `docs/` on GitHub shows only the user pages, so the folder stays wholly user-facing as the role decision records, and no file in it is a maintainer document. The root's 20,000-byte budget carries a fourth folder description, its docs rules included, beside the root files' entries and thirteen pointers; the rules live away from the pages they govern, and the covered folder rule gains a second reason (a user-only folder) beyond a name being taken or rendered, which the check and the root's rules must state.

`docs/README.md` is written as a user page, a short index of the four pages for anyone browsing the folder, rewritten to user content like the rest, so the name counts as taken, and `docs/` is described by the root `CLAUDE.md` with its purpose, rules, and pointers, as the folders whose name is taken are. The check lists `docs/` among the root-described folders and does not read `docs/README.md` as a node, so it is exempt from the node heading check and the node budget. Visitors browsing `docs/` on GitHub get a user-facing orientation to the pages rather than a bare file list or maintainer rules, and the folder stays wholly user content while maintainers still find its rules in the root. It adds a page the role decision does not call for and that duplicates the root `README.md`'s paragraph linking the same pages, and it spends root budget on the description as the reserved-name option does; the check must also tell a user `README.md` from a node in this one folder, the only tracked `README.md` outside the taken or rendered folders that is not a node.

A `docs/README.md` node of the ordinary fixed parts stands in `docs/` and the root points at it, but its purpose part is written so a user browsing the folder reads it as an orientation to the pages, and its pointer notes, to the four pages, serve both readers; only its rules part, the pages' user-only rule and the cut-mechanics rule, is addressed to maintainers. Keeps the covered folder rule and the check unchanged, as the maintainer node does, while softening what GitHub shows a user browsing the folder, and keeps the root's budget free of a `docs/` description. A node is defined as maintainer-facing, so a dual-audience one bends that definition for one folder, and its rules part is still shown to every user browsing `docs/`; the user-facing wording of its purpose and notes is a second voice to keep consistent with the pages each time the update skill touches it.
